items.prompt: In an example test, who chooses the input?
choices: A generator, while the test runs
You, in advance, written into the test
The test runner, picking one at random each run
items.explanation: An example test names its input in the source, so it only ever runs the cases a person wrote down.

items.prompt: Which is a property rather than an example?
choices: Sorting the list 3, 1, 2 returns the list 1, 2, 3 every time
Sorting an empty list returns an empty list again
Sorting any list twice equals sorting it once
items.explanation: A property is a rule about every valid input. The other options each name one specific input.

items.prompt: Six hand-picked tests pass, none with an empty array. What can you conclude about empty arrays?
choices: Nothing, as no test ever tried one
They work, since six tests passed
They work, since arrays of three items work
items.explanation: A passing suite only speaks for the inputs it ran. Untried inputs remain unknown.

items.prompt: What does a property test do that an example test does not?
choices: Replaces the code under test with a copy
Checks a rule against many generated inputs
Runs the same single input a hundred times over
items.explanation: The generator supplies fresh inputs on every run, so one rule is checked against many cases.

items.prompt: `decode(encode(x))` equals `x` is an example of which kind of property?
choices: An idempotence rule: repeat it and nothing changes
A size limit on the encoded output
A round trip: do it, undo it, get the original
items.explanation: Encode followed by decode is a round trip, and the rule says it must return the starting value.

items.prompt: On which attempt did the Scenario's failure appear?
choices: On the 340th case, before the 500 ran out
On the very first case it generated, right away
Only after all 500 cases had been tried
items.explanation: The run failed on attempt 340, well before the 500 cases were used up.

items.prompt: Why did the bug survive six passing examples?
choices: The six tests were written carelessly by the team
No example used the triggering input
The bug only appears when run on slow machines
items.explanation: The bug lives in a single input shape, the empty array, and none of the six examples used it.

items.prompt: A property test replaces which of these?
choices: Every single example test written in the project
The need to write any assertion at all
Choosing inputs by hand, for rule-shaped checks
items.explanation: It changes where inputs come from for checks that have a rule. Example tests still suit cases with no clean rule.

items.prompt: A function has 12 passing example tests. A colleague says it is therefore correct for all inputs. What is the strongest reply?
choices: Twelve examples is only enough if each was written by a different reviewer on the team
Twelve examples cover twelve inputs; a generated-input rule covers many more
The function is correct, because passing tests prove the code for the whole input type
Twelve examples is too few; a hundred hand-written examples would be enough to prove it
items.explanation: Each passing example speaks only for its own input, and a generator tests the same rule against many inputs nobody listed.
items.reference:
Who picks the input?
example test: you pick one input, in advance
property test: you state a rule, a generator picks many
6 examples passed, 500 generated cases found the bug
Why: an example only speaks for the inputs it ran; a property is checked against inputs nobody listed.
items.learnMore:
Examples versus properties

An example pairs one input with one expected output. A property is a rule that must hold for every valid input, and a generator supplies the inputs. The assertion code can look the same; what changes is who chooses the input and how often it runs.

Common mistake

Treating a passing suite as proof for all inputs. It only covers the inputs someone wrote down.
items.reflection: Think of a checklist you run by hand before a trip. Which rule would you want to hold no matter what you pack, and which case did you never think to list?

items.prompt: A test calls `sortTwice([3,1,2])` and expects `[1,2,3]`. Which change turns it into a property test?
choices: Assert that any generated list, sorted twice, equals itself sorted once
Run the same single assertion ten times in a loop, once per run
Add a second hand-picked list holding different numbers and a new expected output
Move the assertion into a shared helper function
items.explanation: The input must become a variable chosen by a generator, and the assertion a rule about every such input.

choices: They have become redundant and should now be deleted from the suite
They are now more reliable than the generated checks, since a person chose them
They can no longer fail, because the property already covers them all
They remain useful as readable, intentional cases
items.explanation: Examples are not made wrong by a property; they stay useful as readable, intentional cases.

items.prompt: Which function is the weakest fit for a property test?
choices: One that serializes a data structure and parses it back again
One that must always return its input list in sorted order
One whose only spec is unrelated special-case outputs
One that has a slow but obviously correct reference version
items.explanation: With no rule beyond a list of unrelated cases, any property would just restate the implementation.

items.prompt: What is a counterexample in property-based testing?
choices: A test that runs more slowly than the others
A property that was written down incorrectly
An input for which the property fails
items.explanation: It is the specific input that broke the rule, which is what the generator is searching for.

items.prompt: What does shrinking do after a failure is found?
choices: Simplifies the failing input while it still fails
Deletes the failing test from the suite entirely
Reruns the very same failing input many times over
items.explanation: Shrinking searches for the smallest version of the input that still reproduces the failure.

items.prompt: Why is a shrunk failure easier to debug than a raw one?
choices: It runs noticeably faster on the test machine
It is small enough to read and reason about
It no longer fails when you rerun it
items.explanation: A tiny failing input leaves fewer places for the cause to hide than a large random blob.

items.prompt: To falsify a property means to...
choices: Prove it holds for all inputs
Delete it from the test suite
Find an input that breaks it
items.explanation: The generator's whole job is to try to falsify the property by finding a counterexample.

items.prompt: The raw failing input is a 40-key nested object. What would shrinking aim to produce?
choices: The smallest input that still fails
A longer input that fails in more ways
A random new input that passes
items.explanation: Shrinking keeps simplified variants only while they still fail, until nothing smaller fails.

items.prompt: A shrinking step produces a simpler input that passes. What happens to that candidate?
choices: It becomes the new reported failure of the whole run
It is discarded; only still-failing inputs are kept
It replaces the property that is under test
items.explanation: A simpler input that passes no longer reproduces the bug, so shrinking drops it and tries another.

items.prompt: The Scenario's report says the failure is on `[]`. Where did `[]` come from?
choices: The author guessed it after reading the code
It was the first input the generator produced
Shrinking reduced a bigger failing input
items.explanation: The tool shrank the failing input until nothing smaller still failed, and that was the empty array.

items.prompt: Which sentence describes the minimal counterexample?
choices: The smallest failing input shrinking reached
The first failing input the generator produced
The input that took the longest time to run
items.explanation: It is what remains once no simpler variant still fails.

items.prompt: A property test reports a counterexample that is a list of 30 mixed objects. Why do tools shrink before reporting?
choices: Large failing inputs are usually false alarms, and shrinking removes them from the report
Shrinking edits the property so it passes with the smaller input in later runs
A small failing input leaves far less code to trace by hand than a large random one
Reporting only small inputs makes the whole test suite run faster overall
items.explanation: The bug is the same, but a small reproduction narrows down where the cause can be.
items.reference:
From raw failure to useful report
raw counterexample: a large random value
try simpler versions, keep any that still fail
stop when nothing smaller fails: the minimal counterexample
Why: a tiny failing input leaves little for the cause to hide behind.
items.learnMore:
Shrinking

A counterexample is an input that breaks the property. Shrinking then tries smaller, simpler variants, keeps the ones that still fail, and reports the smallest it can reach. The result is a bug report you can read, such as an empty array instead of a 40-key blob.

Common mistake

Thinking the raw failing input is the bug. Most of it is usually noise around one small trigger.
items.reflection: Think of a problem you debugged by removing parts until it stopped happening. What was the smallest piece left that still caused it?

items.prompt: During shrinking, a candidate input passes the property. What should the shrinker do with it?
choices: Adopt it as the new failing input and continue shrinking from it
Discard it and try another simplification
Stop and report it as the minimal counterexample found
Mark the property as unreliable and restart the whole run
items.explanation: Only inputs that still fail keep the bug reproduced, so passing candidates are rejected.

Rerun shrinking until a different counterexample appears

items.prompt: Two engineers shrink the same raw failure and get different minimal counterexamples. Which explanation is possible?
choices: One of them must have run the property incorrectly
Shrinking is only valid when every run gives the identical result
The larger of the two results is the one that is correct
Several small inputs trigger the bug, and each reached another
items.explanation: A shrinker stops at what its moves can reach, so more than one minimal input can exist.

items.prompt: `sort(sort(list))` equals `sort(list)`. Which pattern is this?
choices: Idempotence: twice equals once
Round trip: do something and undo it
Oracle comparison against a trusted reference
items.explanation: Sorting twice changes nothing beyond the first sort, which is what idempotence means.

items.prompt: `decode(encode(x))` equals `x`. Which pattern is this?
choices: Idempotence: applying it twice gives the same result
Round trip: do it, then undo it
Invariant under transformation
items.explanation: Encoding followed by decoding must return the starting value, so it is a round trip.

items.prompt: Your fast custom sort must match the built-in sort on every input. Which pattern is this?
choices: Idempotence: sorting twice is the same as sorting once
A round trip with an inverse function
Oracle comparison
items.explanation: The built-in sort acts as the oracle, a simple answer to compare against.

items.prompt: Sorting a list must keep the same length and the same elements. Which pattern is this?
choices: Invariant under transformation
Round trip, using an inverse
Oracle comparison with a slower version
items.explanation: The output order changes but something about it, its contents, never does.

items.prompt: Which property is too weak to catch most bugs on its own?
choices: The round trip returns the original value
The function never throws an error
Sorting twice equals sorting once
items.explanation: A function can return wrong answers without ever throwing, so this check passes anyway.

items.prompt: A property needs to be what kind of statement?
choices: A guess about what the typical input looks like in use
A list of the inputs that happened to be tested
A rule you can state truthfully for every valid input
items.explanation: If the rule is not true for all valid inputs, the property test will fail for the wrong reason.

items.prompt: Why is an oracle usually a simple, slow version?
choices: It is easy to trust, so a mismatch blames the fast one
Slow code is always more reliable than fast code
A faster oracle would make the test run twice as long overall
items.explanation: The oracle exists to be obviously correct. Speed does not matter for it.

items.prompt: Compress then decompress should return the original data. Which pattern is this?
choices: Idempotence: compressing twice is the same
Round trip
Oracle comparison with a trusted compressor
items.explanation: Doing something and then undoing it to get the original back is the round trip pattern.

items.prompt: `reverse(reverse(list))` equals `list`, and `reverse(list)` has the same length as `list`. Which patterns are these?
choices: Idempotence and an oracle comparison against a trusted version
Two round trips, since both involve reversing
An oracle comparison and idempotence
A round trip and an invariant under transformation
items.explanation: Reversing twice undoes the reversal (round trip), and the length is something reversing never changes (invariant).
items.reference:
Four patterns for a property
round trip: do A, undo A, get the original
idempotence: twice equals once
invariant: something about the output never changes
oracle: matches a simple, trusted version
Why: a good property says something true about the output, not only that nothing crashed.
items.learnMore:
Writing a property

Look for a rule that is always true: an inverse, a repeat that changes nothing, a quantity that never changes, or a slow trusted version to compare with. Pick one you can check without re-implementing the function.

Common mistake

Using 'it never throws' as the whole property. A function that returns wrong answers quietly still passes it.
items.reflection: Pick a tool you use that has an 'undo' or a 'repeat does nothing' behaviour. Which of the four patterns describes it?

items.prompt: A function `normalizeEmail` lowercases and trims an address. Which property is the best fit?
choices: Normalizing twice always throws an error
Normalizing returns a longer string each time it is applied
Normalizing an already normalized address changes nothing
Normalizing a valid address returns an empty string every time
items.explanation: Applying it a second time must make no further change, which is idempotence.

items.prompt: A developer writes the property `fastSort(list)` never throws. The function returns `[]` for every input. What does the property report?
choices: A failure, since returning `[]` counts as an exception
A pass, because it never throws, though outputs are wrong
A failure, because the output length differs from the input
A pass only if the generated list was also empty
items.explanation: Never throwing is satisfied by wrong answers, which makes the property too weak by itself.

items.prompt: A new fast `dedupe(list)` has complex rules, and a slow nested-loop version is trusted. Which property gives the most coverage for the least effort?
choices: Compare `dedupe` against the trusted slow version on generated lists
Check that `dedupe` returns a list for every generated input
Check that `dedupe` runs in less than one second on a typical small generated list
Check that `dedupe` is called with a list
items.explanation: The oracle supplies the expected answer for every generated input without hand-computed values.

items.prompt: What does a generator produce?
choices: The expected output for each test
Test inputs of a chosen type
A copy of the code under test
items.explanation: A generator creates the values that the property is checked against.

items.prompt: Why do good generators produce edge cases like `0` and the empty string often?
choices: They make the tests finish faster
They are the only valid values for those types
People forget them, and bugs hide there
items.explanation: Humans skip values that feel abnormal, so generators deliberately over-produce them.

items.prompt: How is a generator for an object with a name and an age usually built?
choices: By combining a string and a number generator
By calling the real function and copying its output
By using one fixed object every single time
items.explanation: Generators compose the way the type itself is made from fields.

items.prompt: 100 generated runs all pass. What does that show?
choices: The property holds for every possible input
No counterexample turned up in 100 tries
The code has no bugs left in it
items.explanation: It is a search for a failure, not a proof, and the search came up empty.

items.prompt: Does raising the number of runs from 100 to 1000 help?
choices: No, a pass at 100 already means the code is proven
Yes, but only if the generator is replaced first
Yes, it raises the chance of hitting a rare bug
items.explanation: More runs search more of the input space, though never all of it.

items.prompt: A bug appears on about 1 case in 340. About how likely is it to be found in 100 runs?
choices: About 25 percent
About 100 percent, since 100 is a large number
About 1 percent, since runs barely matter
items.explanation: The chance of at least one hit in 100 runs works out to roughly 25.5 percent.

items.prompt: Which step comes right after a property check fails in the loop?
choices: Starting the whole run over silently
Shrinking the failing input
Ignoring that run and continuing on
items.explanation: A failure leads straight to shrinking toward the smallest failing input.

items.prompt: When does the loop report a pass?
choices: When the first run passes
When shrinking finds a smaller failing input
When every configured run comes back clean
items.explanation: Only after every one of the N runs came back clean does the tool report a pass.

items.prompt: A generator picks integers uniformly from 0 to 1,000,000 to test a function that has a bug whenever the input is 0. Roughly how likely is one run to hit it?
choices: About one in a million, so it will usually be missed
About one in two, since 0 is the smallest possible value
Certain, because 0 is always generated before any other value
About one in a hundred, which makes it a common case
items.explanation: A uniform pick almost never lands on 0, which is why generators bias toward it.
items.reference:
Generate, check, shrink
1 run at 1 in 340: about 0.3 percent to hit the bug
100 runs: about 25.5 percent
500 runs: about 77.1 percent
1000 runs: about 94.7 percent
Why: a pass means no counterexample was found, which is evidence and never proof.
items.learnMore:
Generators and runs

Generators produce inputs and are biased toward edge cases like zero, empty and duplicates. The loop generates, checks and, on failure, shrinks. More runs raise the chance of hitting a rare bug but never reach certainty. The percentages assume independent cases at the observed 1-in-340 rate.

Common mistake

Reading a pass as proof. It only reports that the search found nothing.
items.reflection: Think of a search you gave up on after finding nothing. How long would you have needed to look before being confident nothing was there?

items.prompt: A bug appears on about 1 generated case in 340. Ten runs pass. What is the sound conclusion?
choices: The bug is absent, because ten clean runs are enough to rule it out entirely
The bug is ten times less likely than first assumed
The generator is broken and should be rewritten from scratch
The bug is likely still hiding
items.explanation: Ten runs give only about a 3 percent chance of a hit, so a pass is weak evidence.

items.prompt: A team raises runs from 500 to 1000 for a bug that appears 1 case in 340. About how does the chance of finding it change?
choices: From about 50 percent to about 100 percent, certain at last
From about 25 percent to about 50 percent, a clean doubling
From about 77 percent to about 95 percent

items.explanation: Using the assumed rate, 500 runs give 77.1 percent and 1000 runs give 94.7 percent.

items.prompt: Write `isRoundTrip(encode, decode, x)`. It returns true when `decode(encode(x))` equals `x` (compare with `JSON.stringify`), otherwise false.

tests.description: a codec that breaks empty arrays fails

items.explanation: Run the pair on x and compare the result with x. Comparing the JSON text handles arrays and objects, and an `undefined` result never matches a real value.

items.prompt: Write `isIdempotent(fn, x)`. It returns true when `fn(fn(x))` equals `fn(x)` (compare with `JSON.stringify`).

tests.description: reversing twice is not the same as once

items.explanation: Idempotence means applying the function a second time changes nothing, so compare the result of one application with the result of two.

items.prompt: Write `keepsLength(fn, list)`. It returns true when `fn(list)` has the same length as `list`.
items.explanation: A length check is a simple invariant under transformation: the order may change but the count must not.

items.prompt: Write `isSortedAscending(list)`. It returns true when every item is less than or equal to the next. An empty or one-item list counts as sorted.
items.explanation: Compare each neighbouring pair. A list with fewer than two items has no pair to violate the rule, so it is sorted.

items.prompt: Write `hasNoDuplicates(list)`. It returns true when no value appears twice in a list of numbers or strings.
items.explanation: A Set drops repeats, so its size equals the list length exactly when there were no repeats.

items.prompt: Write `sameElements(a, b)`. It returns true when `a` and `b` contain the same numbers the same number of times, in any order.
items.explanation: Sort copies of both lists and compare. Two lists are the same multiset exactly when their sorted forms match.

items.prompt: Write `matchesOracle(mySort, list)`. It returns true when `mySort` on a copy of `list` equals the built-in numeric sort `[...list].sort((a, b) => a - b)` (compare with `JSON.stringify`).
items.explanation: The built-in sort plays the oracle. Passing a copy to mySort keeps the original list intact for the comparison.

items.prompt: Write `neverIncreases(applyDiscount, price, code)`. It returns true when `applyDiscount(price, code)` is at most `price`.

tests.description: a buggy discount that adds money

items.explanation: Total after a discount may not exceed the total before one. That one-line invariant needs no knowledge of how the discount is computed.

items.prompt: Write `isSortedAndNonOverlapping(intervals)`. Each interval is `{ start, end }`. Return true when the list is in increasing order of start and no two neighbours share a point, so each `start` must be greater than the previous `end`. Empty and one-item lists return true.

tests.description: touching at a point counts as sharing

items.explanation: If every start is strictly greater than the previous end, the list is both in order and free of shared points. The first range has no previous one, so the loop starts at 1.
items.reference:
Turn a rule into a check
state the rule in plain words first
compute from the input only, then compare to the output
test it on a case that should pass and one that should fail
Why: a property check is a function that returns true or false for one input.
items.learnMore:
Writing property checks

Each check takes the function under test and one input, applies the rule, and returns a boolean. Test the check itself with a pass case and a fail case, so you know it can actually fail.

Common mistake

Writing a check that cannot fail, such as comparing a value with itself.
items.reflection: Think of a rule you rely on in daily life. How would you check it on one case, and how would you know your check could actually fail?

items.prompt: Write `coversSamePoints(input, output)`. Both are lists of `{ start, end }` ranges with integer bounds. Return true when the set of integer points covered by `input` (every integer from start to end, inclusive) equals the set covered by `output`.

tests.expr: expect(coversSamePoints([{ start: 1, end: 3 }, { start: 2, end: 6 }], [{ start: 1, end: 6 }])).toBe(true)
expect(coversSamePoints([{ start: 1, end: 10 }, { start: 2, end: 3 }], [{ start: 1, end: 3 }])).toBe(false)

items.explanation: List every covered integer into a Set for each side and compare the sets. Sizes differing catches lost or invented points; the membership loop catches the same size with different points.

items.prompt: Write `firstFailingInput(property, inputs)`. It tries each input in order and returns the first one for which `property(input)` is false, or `null` when every input passes.

tests.description: returns the input, not its index

items.explanation: This is the core of a property run: try inputs one at a time and stop at the first counterexample. Returning the input itself, not its index, is what a shrinker would start from.

items.prompt: Write `shrinkOnce(items, stillFails)`. Try removing one item at a time, from the first position to the last. Return the first shorter list (with that one item removed) for which `stillFails(list)` is true. If no shorter list still fails, or removing would leave an empty list, return `items` unchanged.

tests.description: later item removed when earlier ones are needed

items.explanation: One shrinking step: for each position, build the list without that item and keep it only if the failure persists. Repeating this step until it returns the same list reaches a minimal failing input.

items.prompt: What does mergeIntervals do with the ranges 1-4 and 3-6?
choices: Merges them into one range, 1-6
Keeps them as two separate ranges, untouched
Returns only the second range, 3-6
items.explanation: The two ranges overlap, so they combine into a single range covering both.

items.prompt: In the buggy code, what is wrong with `last.end = curr.end`?
choices: It should keep the smaller of the two ends
It should keep the larger of the two ends
It should add the two ends together
items.explanation: When the new range is inside the old one, its end is smaller and overwrites the wider end.

items.prompt: Which input did the four example tests never try?
choices: Two ranges that overlap each other
Two ranges that do not touch at all
A range fully inside another range
items.explanation: In all four examples each new range ended later than the last, so containment was untested.

items.prompt: Which is a coverage-preserving property?
choices: The output covers the same points as the input
The output always has fewer ranges than the input
The output is always a single range
items.explanation: Merging must neither lose nor invent points, only join ranges.

items.prompt: After merging, no two output ranges should do what?
choices: Have different lengths
Share a point
Start on even numbers
items.explanation: If two output ranges shared a point, they should have been merged into one.

items.prompt: The raw failing list had 4 ranges. How many did the minimal counterexample have?
choices: Three ranges
Four ranges
Two ranges
items.explanation: Shrinking removed two ranges and ended at a pair, one inside the other.

items.prompt: Which shrinking move did the trace use first?
choices: Removing a whole range
Tightening one bound by one
Reordering the list
items.explanation: Removing a range is the biggest simplification, so it comes first.

items.prompt: How does the minimal counterexample 12-13 with 12-12 point at the bug?
choices: The two ranges do not overlap at all
The end 13 is lost when 12-12 overwrites it
Both ranges happen to start on the same even number
items.explanation: The output covers only up to 12, so the larger end 13 disappeared, exposing the overwrite.

items.prompt: `mergeIntervals` turns 1-10 and 2-3 into 1-3. Which property does this output violate?
choices: Sorted: the output ranges are out of order
Non-overlap: the two output ranges share a point
Coverage: points 4 to 10 were lost
Length: the output has more ranges than the input does
items.explanation: The output is one range 1-3, in order and not overlapping, but it covers fewer points than the input.
items.reference:
The contained interval
1-10 and 2-3 should merge to 1-10
the buggy line gives 1-3 and loses points 4 to 10
4 examples walked forward; none was contained
shrink: 4 ranges, 3, then 2, then tighten to 12-13 with 12-12
Why: taking the new end differs from taking the larger end only when the new range is inside the old one.
items.learnMore:
The mergeIntervals case

Three invariants hold for any correct output: sorted, non-overlapping, and covering exactly the points the input covered. The buggy loop keeps the new end instead of the larger end, so a contained range truncates the merge. Shrinking walks a four-range failure down to two ranges, one inside the other.

Common mistake

Assuming the raw failure shows what is needed. Two of its four ranges were irrelevant.
items.reflection: Think of a rule you apply that works until one case where the new item is 'inside' the old one. What would that case look like in your work?

items.prompt: Why did all four example tests pass with the buggy line?
choices: The sort step already merged the ranges before the loop ran
Each new range ended later, so its end was the larger one
The buggy line was never executed by any of the tests
The bug cancelled out with a second, hidden bug in the sort
items.explanation: Taking the new end only differs from taking the larger end when the new range is contained.

items.prompt: The shrinker has a failing pair, 3-17 and 12-14, and tightens bounds one unit at a time. What stops it at 12-13 and 12-12?
choices: Every smaller candidate passes the property
It reaches the maximum number of steps it is allowed
The generator forbids ranges shorter than one unit
The property is changed to be easier to satisfy
items.explanation: A shrinker stops when every smaller candidate passes the property.

items.prompt: Why is `formatCurrency(4210)` returning `"$42.10"` a poor fit for a property test?
choices: It has no inputs at all
No rule simpler than the code itself
It always throws an error on any input
items.explanation: With no clean invariant, an example test is the better tool.

items.prompt: What is wrong with a generator that is too narrow?
choices: It runs far too many tests every single time
It produces values of the wrong type
It cannot produce inputs where bugs live
items.explanation: A test's reach is limited to what its generator can produce.

items.prompt: What is wrong with a generator that is too broad?
choices: It wastes runs on inputs nobody could send
It finds fewer bugs overall
It cannot be combined with other generators
items.explanation: Many runs on invalid inputs, like a range starting after it ends, add no value.

items.prompt: A precondition filter is used to do what?
choices: Make every generated input larger
Discard inputs that are not valid
Repeat the same input twice in a row
items.explanation: It skips inputs that fall outside what the function should handle.

items.prompt: A failure that shows up 1 run in 500 looks like what?
choices: A passing test
A syntax error in the property
A flaky test
items.explanation: A rare failure resembles non-determinism, though the cause is the random input.

items.prompt: How do you make a rare random failure repeatable?
choices: Record the random seed used
Run the test far fewer times than before
Delete the generator
items.explanation: Replaying the same seed regenerates the exact failing input.

items.prompt: If a generator never makes a zero-length range, what can it never find?
choices: Bugs that occur for long ranges
Bugs tied to zero-length ranges
Bugs caused by overlapping ranges
items.explanation: A shape the generator cannot produce can never be tested.

items.prompt: Do more runs fix a narrow generator?
choices: Yes, with enough runs they eventually cover every shape
Yes, but only above 1000 runs
No, they repeat the same limited shapes
items.explanation: A narrow generator keeps sampling the same reachable space, however many times.

items.prompt: A generator for `mergeIntervals` picks starts and ends from 0 to 1,000,000. After many runs nothing fails. What is the likely issue?
choices: The property is too strong to ever fail on any input
The function under test is certainly correct by now
The generator produces too many edge cases for the function
Ranges rarely overlap, so merging is barely exercised
items.explanation: Huge ranges rarely touch, so a bug that needs overlap or containment is almost never reached.
items.reference:
When a property test misleads
no rule: keep example tests
too narrow: bugs outside its reach never appear
too broad: runs wasted on invalid inputs, add a filter
rare failure: record the seed to replay it
Why: a property test reaches only what its generator can produce, however many runs it makes.
items.learnMore:
Generator limits

A generator shapes what the test can find. Too narrow and it misses shapes; too broad and runs are spent on inputs no caller could send. Not every function has a clean rule, and a rare failure should be made repeatable with the random seed.

Common mistake

Believing that more runs repair a generator that cannot make the failing shape.
items.reflection: Think of a survey or sample that missed an important group. What did the way it was sampled leave out?

items.prompt: A generator sometimes produces a range whose start is after its end, which the function does not accept. Which fix keeps every run meaningful?
choices: Remove the property so invalid ranges cannot fail it
Lower the number of runs until none appears
Add a precondition so only valid ranges are kept
Make the function accept any range at all
items.explanation: Filtering invalid inputs keeps every run testing something the function is meant to handle.
